context: There are 5 items, and the knapsack capacity is cap = 50. The table gives the item data. You may take up to the full weight of each item or divide it and take any fraction. You receive the same fraction of its original value.
description: The table on the left lists item number i, weight wgt[i-1], and value val[i-1], with a fruit icon for each item. The banana in row 2 is highlighted in pale pink and the pineapple in row 4 in pale orange. The “Weight taken” column shows 20 and 30 respectively. An unlabeled arrow leads from each row to the knapsack on the right, whose capacity is 50. The bottom shows the optimal selection and its value.

The first three columns reproduce the diagram's data, with fruit names taken from the icons. The additional unit value column divides value by weight. For example, the apple's unit value is 50 ÷ 10 = 5.

frames.explanation: The whole banana weighs 20 and contributes 120 in value, leaving room for 30. The whole pineapple weighs 40, so take three quarters of it for a value of (30/40) × 210 = 157.5. The maximum value shown at the bottom is 120 + (30/40) × 210 = 277.5. Together the portions weigh 20 + 30 = 50. No other items are taken.
frames.title: Example data for fractional knapsack

summary: In the optimal solution shown, a knapsack of capacity 50 holds the whole banana and part of the pineapple.
